transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Ryland Barton.
A teacher's actions likely helped save lives
during a school shooting that killed three children
and one teacher in Bend, Oregon yesterday.
Bend police chief Mike Krantz called her actions heroic.
- A teacher in the classroom threw her cell phone
at the suspect and then tackled him
and fought to take the firearm from him.
She was not injured in that incident,
but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed.
- The gunman was shot and killed by a father
who followed him into the building.
Krantz identified the attacker
as a 16-year-old former student at the school
and said all the victims were shot in the same classroom.
The shooter fired as many as 15 rounds
from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining.
President Trump told reporters he didn't order restrictions
on a satellite communication system
that's used by Ukraine's military,
cutting connections to some of its drones.
- Trump also said he doubted the disruption came from Elon Musk,
who owns Star Shield, SpaceX's military-grade version
of the Starlink satellite internet service.
The sudden restrictions alarmed Ukraine's military
and government officials this week,
with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
The White House says its newest press secretary is out.
NPR's Emily Fang reports that Katie Zachariah
was just days into the job.
- Asked by reporters about Zachariah,
President Trump said he gave her the option to quit.
- I said, "Katie, you know, you don't have to do this.
You know, she said this is a lot tougher."
I said, "Welcome to the world of Trump."
- Zachariah has been careful to describe herself as a lawyer,
not an attorney, and she ultimately admitted
that she failed the California bar exam,
meaning she is not licensed to practice law,
though Trump has referred to her as an attorney before.
Zachariah initially seemed to sidestep questions
about the bar exam, saying repeatedly that she moved to China,
where she practiced law with "all appropriate credentials."
Zachariah later said she misheard the question.
Emily Fang and Pure News Washington.
- Despite powerful new ways to protect newborn babies
against the dangerous respiratory virus RSV,
many infants are still at risk, and PR's Rob Stein reports.
- RSV sends tens of thousands of babies
to the hospital each year.
Many end up fighting for their lives in intensive care.
The best way to protect infants is to immunize newborns
before they are discharged from hospitals.
But insurance companies typically won't pay
for the shots in the hospital.
They're only required to pay for them in doctor's offices.
So about half of babies are being left unprotected
against RSV, which is on the rise again right now.
Rob Stein and Pure News.
- Several brush fires are burning in Southern California,
stoked by hot, windy weather that's led to evacuations
and caused utility companies to shut off electricity
for tens of thousands of people around the state.
Weather conditions that increase the fire risk
are expected to last through tomorrow.
Stock market closed lower on Wall Street today.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The U.S. is attempting to revive
three shuttered nuclear plants to meet growing demand,
especially from data centers.
It's unprecedented.
No nuclear reactor has resumed generating electricity
after being decommissioned.
The federal government's lending up to $4.4 billion
to restart plants in Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Iowa.
Number of people facing life-threatening hunger
has doubled over the past decade,
according to a new analysis.
NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports food crises
in just three countries account for much of that toll.
- 266 million people worldwide are facing acute hunger,
according to a report from the nonprofit
Action Against Hunger.
About a third of them live in the Democratic Republic
of Congo, Sudan, and Nigeria.
Conflict is a major cause of the crisis.
Ongoing fighting is displacing millions of people
while making it harder to deliver humanitarian aid.
Climate change is playing a role too,
with disasters destroying crops and livelihoods.
And rising poverty in some countries
is putting food out of reach for many.
This increase in hunger is happening as funds to fight it
drop.
Humanitarian aid targeting food insecurity
fell by nearly 60% over the past few years.
The authors say that peace and more funding
are needed to reverse the trend.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
- The NBA is restricting certain types of betting
following scandals that led to arrests
of current and former NBA figures.
It includes bets on which player
records the first stat of a game
and the outcome of the opening tip.
The league also requires players, coaches, and staff
to attend in-person training on sports betting rules.
I'm Ryland Barton, this is NPR News.
This message comes from Bombas.

cool weather calls for cozier footwear.

all with layers of cloud-like cushioning.

topics.text: Teacher threw phone and tackled gunman during Bend, Oregon school shooting that killed four
Father shot and killed the 16-year-old Bend shooter who followed him into the building
Trump says he didn't order restrictions on Starlink-type satellite system used by Ukraine's military
White House press secretary Katie Zachariah departs after just days on the job
Infants remain at risk from RSV because insurers often don't cover shots given in hospitals
Brush fires burn in Southern California, prompting evacuations and utility power shutoffs
U.S. government lends $4.4 billion to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet data center demand
Number of people facing life-threatening hunger doubles over past decade, led by Congo, Sudan, Nigeria
NBA restricts certain bets, including first-stat and opening-tip wagers, after betting scandals and arrests
Stock market closes lower on Wall Street
